newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq confrontation appears to ease, Kurds clash.
newsitem.headline: Iraq confrontation appears to ease, Kurds clash.

text.p: Rival Kurdish factions skirmished in northern Iraq as the United States appeared to back away from further air strikes to punish Iraq for an offensive against Kurdish rebels.
Kurdish fighters exchanged small arms and mortar fire on Thursday south of Arbil, the city seized by one Kurdish faction with the help of Iraq troops from a rival group last Saturday.

Iraqi tanks were positioned about 15 km (nine miles) outside Arbil but no Iraqi troops could be seen in the city, the centre of a Kurdish administration set up after the 1991 Gulf War as a "safe haven" to protect Kurds from attacks by the Iraqi army.
In Washington, U.S. intelligence chief John Deutch told the Senate Intelligence Committee that Iraqi troops were now pulling out of northern Iraq.
"We are seeing the withdrawal of the mechanised and armoured units from the Kurdish territories in northern Iraq back to their garrisons fairly systematically," Deutch said.

Iraq's military action to help the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) to wrest control of Arbil from the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) triggered U.S. cruise missile attacks on air defence installations in southern Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the United States reserved the right to strike at Iraq again if Baghdad tried to re-build the air defences disabled by the U.S. raids.
The air strikes drew varying reactions from European countries, with Britain and Germany lining up behind Washington and France, Spain and Italy withholding endorsement.

France said it would stay in the U.S.-led Gulf War alliance patrolling "no-fly" zones in northern and southern Iraq, but it would not helpt to police an enlarged zone declared in the south by U.S. President Bill Clinton.
In Baghdad, thousands of Arab residents of Iraq, carrying portraits of President Saddam Hussein, demonstrated against the cruise missile raids and burned an effigy of Clinton.

"Your aggression on Iraq is an aggression against the whole Arab nation," chanted the demonstrators, most of whom came from Yemen, Sudan, Jordan and Tunisia -- countries which sympathised with Baghdad during the Gulf War that ejected Iraqi troops from Kuwait.
The Iraqi government has vowed to ignore the no-fly zones in northern and southern Iraq, but the state-controlled press toned down its previous defiant anti-U.S. rhetoric.

Newspapers carried front-page pictures of Saddam meeting his military commanders and printed pictures inside of casualties suffered in the U.S. strikes raids on military targets in southern Iraq by a total of 44 cruise missiles.

A government spokesman, speaking after Saddam chaired a meeting of top officials, said Iraq would consider the U.S. military action had ended only when U.S. planes stopped violating Iraq's airspace and threatening its sovereignty.

Despite the U.S. and Iraqi assertions that Iraqi troops were pulling back from northern Iraq, PUK leader Jalal Talabani said in an interview that he still faced a joint Iraqi-KDP offensive and would seek Iranian help if necessary.

"We will call support from any country which is ready to help us -- from Iran, Syria or Turkey," he said in Sulaimaniya, his stronghold near the Iranian border. "There is no possibility of peace now in this region."

Turkey indicated that it might move forces into northern Iraq to stop anti-Ankara Kurdish separatists of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) from using the region as a springboard for attacks in southeast Turkey.

"There is the possibility of a sudden air-backed assault into northern Iraq. We are thinking of hitting the enemy (PKK) all of a sudden without giving it the chance of protection," said a senior military official, who declined to be identified.

Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said later a cross-border operation was not imminent, although a cabinet minister was quoted as saying Turkey had asked Iraq for understanding over possible incursions into its territory to thwart Kurdish rebels.
